title: PCSK9 inhibitors: what we know, what we should have understood, and what is to come.

PCSK9 inhibitors: what we know, what we
should have understood, and what is to come
Marc S. Sabatine
*
TIMI Study Group, Division of Cardiovascular Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA
This editorial refers to ‘Efficacy and safety of alirocumab
and evolocumab: a systematic review and meta-analysis of
randomized controlled trials’, by P. Guedeney et al.,
doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehz430.
Currently, two PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin
type 9) inhibitors are available for clinical use: evolocumab and aliro-
cumab. Both are fully human monoclonal antibodies and both were
studied in very large, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled,
cardiovascular outcomes trials, which were entitled FOURIER and
ODYSSEY Outcomes, respectively. Both trials enrolled very high-
risk patients with ‘hard’ established atherosclerotic cardiovascular
disease: prior myocardial infarction (MI), non-haemorrhagic stroke,
or symptomatic peripheral artery disease in the case of FOURIER,
and prior MI in ODYSSEY Outcomes.
In both trials, the main objectives were achieved, and the PCSK9
inhibitors were shown to significantly reduce the risk of the primary
endpoints. Specifically, in FOURIER, evolocumab reduced the risk of
a broad quintuple primary endpoint (a composite consisting of car-
diovascular death, MI, stroke, hospitalization for unstable angina, or
coronary revascularization) by 15% and the harder key secondary
endpoint of cardiovascular death, MI, or stroke by 20%.1 In
ODYSSEY Outcomes, alirocumab reduced the risk of death from
coronary heart disease, MI, ischaemic stroke, or unstable angina
requiring hospitalization by 15%.2 More specifically, in both trials,
there were clear, significant reductions in the risk of MI (27% with
evolocumab and 14% with alirocumab), ischaemic stroke (25% and
27%, respectively), and coronary revascularization (22% and 12%,
respectively).
In this issue of the European Heart Journal, Guedeney and col-
leagues present a meta-analysis of the effect of evolocumab and aliro-
cumab on cardiovascular outcomes, combining data from 39 phase II
or phase III randomized controlled trials and totalling 66 478
patients.3 Although they included a large number of trials, the sheer
size of FOURIER and ODYSSEY Outcomes means that those two tri-
als completely dominated their analysis and accounted for >95% of
the events. Thus, not surprisingly, the meta-analysed effect of PCSK9
inhibition on MI, ischaemic stroke, and coronary revascularization
(20, 22, and 17% relative risk reductions, respectively) are quite close
to what one might estimate from simply averaging the effect
observed in FOURIER and ODYSSEY Outcomes. Likewise, no major
safety issues emerged in either FOURIER or ODYSSEY Outcomes,
and thus no major safety issues were seen in the meta-analysis,
including a risk ratio (RR) of 1.00 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.93–
1.07] for new-onset diabetes.
Guedeney et al. note that there was no significant effect of PCSK9
inhibition on cardiovascular death (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.84–1.06). Some
people had expected to see a reduction in cardiovascular mortality.
To that end, in the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists Collaboration of
statin trials, there was a 12% reduction in cardiovascular mortality for
each 1 mmol/L reduction in LDL cholesterol (LDL-C).4 In FOURIER
and ODYSSEY Outcomes, treatment with evolocumab and alirocu-
mab resulted in 1.38 and 1.24 mmol/L reductions in LDL-C, respect-
ively, at 1 year. Based on those numbers, should we have expected
15–16% reductions in cardiovascular mortality in these trials? I think
not.
We also know from the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists
Collaboration that there is a lag before LDL-C lowering translates
into a clinical benefit (Take home figure). For the composite of major
vascular events, the lag tends to be 6 months or so, translating into
the benefit from LDL-C lowering in the first year being about half of
what is seen in subsequent years.4 The lag for a reduction in fatal out-
comes seems even longer. 4S and LIPID are two statin trials that pub-
lished cumulative incidence curves for the successful reduction of a
pre-specified fatal primary endpoint (all-cause mortality and death
from coronary heart disease, respectively). For both trials, the event
curves appear to start to diverge at 1.5 years.5,6 Faced with intense
pressure to provide cardiovascular outcomes data, the sponsors of
both trials (Amgen and Sanofi & Regeneron) opted to have larger tri-
als with shorter durations in order to accrue events more quickly. In
FOURIER, the median duration of follow-up was only 2.2 years; in
ODYSSEY Outcomes, it was a bit longer at 2.8 years.

Taking the relatively short duration of these two trials into ac-
count, what effect on cardiovascular mortality might we have realis-
tically expected to see in those trials? In FOURIER, on average only
the last 32% of a patient’s time in the trial was after 1.5 years; in
ODYSSEY Outcomes it was the last 45% of their time. Based on
those proportions of time, we might have therefore expected only a
5% reduction in cardiovascular mortality in FOURIER and 7% in
ODYSSEY Outcomes, the average of which is 6%—exactly the num-
ber seen in this meta-analysis.
Further supporting the notion that PCSK9 inhibitors should ultim-
ately reduce cardiovascular mortality are data from Mendelian ran-
domization studies. We have shown that for genetically mediated
lifelong lower LDL-C, whether mediated through variants in the gene
encoding HMG-CoA reductase (the target of statins) or in the gene
encoding PCSK9, the odds ratio per unit reduction in LDL-C for a
composite of major cardiovascular events as well as for death from
coronary heart disease individually were virtually identical regardless
of which gene was involved.7 This observation stands to reason as it
is hard to conceive of an intervention that would lower the risk of MI
and of stroke but not, with sufficient time and events, lower the risk
of death from those events.
Nonetheless, additional longer term cardiovascular outcomes tri-
als addressing this issue will be valuable. Two trials are underway that
should shed additional light. The first trial is HPS4/TIMI 65/ORION-4,
which is studying inclisiran, an experimental small interfering RNA
against PCSK9. The trial aims to enrol 15 000 patients with prior
MI, prior stroke, or peripheral artery disease, and to have a median
duration of follow-up 4–5 years.8 The second trial is VESALIUS-CV,
which is studying evolocumab. The trial aims to enrol 13 000
patients at somewhat lower risk than the prior trials. Specifically,
VESALIUS-CV is targeting patients without a history of MI or stroke,
but who have stable atherosclerosis or diabetes mellitus.9 The me-
dian duration of follow-up is also expected to be 4–5 years.
As a field, we should be proud of the remarkable progress we have
made in lipid-lowering therapy. The 4S trial starting enrolling patients
just over 30 years ago. At the time, there was clinical equipoise
regarding whether a patient with a prior MI would benefit from low-
ering an LDL-C of 4.9 mmol/L. Thanks to the dedication of large
number of investigators and an even larger number of patients, we
now know that there is consistent clinical benefit in lowering LDL-C
down to levels <0.5 mmol/L.10,11 We have the knowledge and we
have the tools. I am optimistic that the next round of clinical trials will
provide the data to propel us further in taking the necessary action to
prevent the ravages of atherosclerosis in our patients.
